newspapers and magazines, and enterprise. This study also considers variation in users’ 
app consumption habits across categories, using third-party research. For example, 
consumers often listen to audiobooks through apps on mobile devices, but are more 
likely to stream videos on smart TVs. Additionally, when the data is available, variation in 
the consumption patterns of iOS (and non-iOS) users by app type is taken into account. 
Estimates of total sales rely on inputs from third-party sources, typically market research 
firms.xix The sales are apportioned using the share of content consumed in apps on any 
platform, based on information collected from marketing surveys, company reports, or 
data on usage patterns.xx Finally, usage is apportioned to Apple iOS devices specifically 
using the iOS market share for each device category in each respective country.xxi
Enterprise apps, which allow businesses and organizations to provide tools and 
capabilities on smartphones and tablets, are treated differently than consumer apps. 
Usage patterns are more heterogeneous for enterprise apps than for consumer apps, and 
app- and desktop-based usage of enterprise products tend to be more integrated.  We 
estimate sales separately for major enterprise apps or families of apps – Microsoft Office 
365, Google Workspace (i.e., enterprise versions of Google productivity tools such as 
Gmail and Google Docs), Adobe (Acrobat), Dropbox, Box, Webex, Zoom, and Slack. We 
also include an aggregate market-level estimate for mobility management apps, which 
allow employees to securely access business content.
Sales of physical goods and services through the app
Many developers monetize their apps by selling physical products through their apps. 
These include:
	
˿
Apps that let customers purchase physical goods and services. This study broadly 
refers to these as m-commerce apps.9 The group includes apps for general retail, 
ride hailing, food delivery and pickup, grocery delivery, and travel.
	
˿
Apps that enable digital payments or transfers, such as peer-to-peer transfer apps.
M-commerce
Globally, mobile apps have become an increasingly popular e-commerce channel. Apps 
from retailers such as Amazon and Target allow consumers to browse and purchase 
physical goods directly in the app and arrange for delivery. In addition, mobile apps – 
including those for ride hailing, food delivery and pickup, grocery delivery and pickup, 
and mobile pickup ordering – have been central to the creation or expansion of certain 
business models.
Sales on m-commerce apps do not occur through Apple’s in-app purchase system.10 
Third-party data are used to estimate the volume of sales of physical goods and services 
from transactions on mobile apps.11 Results are provided for several categories of apps: 
general retail, food delivery and pickup, travel, grocery, and ride hailing.
9	
M-commerce refers to the buying or selling of goods and services on mobile devices, either through mobile apps or 
mobile browsers.
10	 Since the launch of the App Store, Apple’s policy has been to not charge a commission on sales of physical goods and 
services.
11	 The sales associated with purchases made on mobile browser apps are excluded.


---

16
Apple's Global App Store Ecosystem and Its Growth, 2025
For many of the m-commerce categories, this study relies on Statista’s Digital Market 
Outlook and Mobility Market Outlook data for online sales revenue. In 2022, Statista 
updated its methodology for estimating industry revenues by using current exchange 
rates, rather than fixed exchange rates, with the goal of being more accurate. As a result, 
its estimates for all years, including 2019 and 2024, were retroactively updated. 
For general retail, total m-commerce sales estimates are based on EMARKETER data. 
For grocery in the US, total e-commerce sales estimates are also based on EMARKETER 
data. In 2025, EMARKETER updated its methodology for estimating e-commerce and 
m-commerce. As a result, its estimates for 2019 were retroactively updated. EMARKETER 
periodically updates its estimates for several reasons, including, but not limited to, 
incorporating new, higher-quality data sources, adjusting the weights assigned to different 
sources, and refreshing foreign exchange assumptions (i.e., changing the base year used 
in currency conversions).
For each app category, the total volume of e-commerce or m-commerce sales relies on 
estimates from third-party sources, typically market research firms.xxii This study then 
apportions the volume of sales, if necessary, to purchases that occur via smartphone 
and tablet apps. For example, for online food delivery and pickup, customers may 
place orders via an app, a mobile browser, or a desktop browser. The share of each app 
category’s sales that occurs via mobile apps is estimated using information collected 
from marketing surveys or data on usage patterns.xxiii Finally, usage attributable to Apple 
platforms is apportioned based on the overall iOS market share.12,xxiv 
Digital payments
Digital payment apps continue to become increasingly popular worldwide, although the 
landscape differs substantially across countries. In China, currently the largest market for 
digital payments, two QR code-based payment apps, Alipay and WeChat Pay, dominate 
both online and brick-and-mortar points of sale. These apps charge merchants a fee on 
purchases paid for with their apps. In the US, peer-to-peer transfer apps such as Venmo 
and Cash App are already popular and have grown significantly in recent years. 
This study estimates transaction fees collected by developers from customers or 
merchants for payments and transfers made through apps on the iOS platform.13 For 
peer-to-peer transfer apps in the US, we use the ratio of total transaction fees to total 
payment volume (TPV) from Venmo and Cash App to estimate the transaction fees 
collected by the apps. For QR code-based payment apps in China, we start with an 
estimate of TPV from a third-party research firm. We then estimate WeChat Pay and 
Alipay total transaction fees using their published fee rates and deductible policies. 
Finally, we apportion usage to Apple platforms based on data on the overall iOS share in 
each region.
In-app advertising
In-app advertising is a frequently used and effective method of monetizing apps whereby 
developers publish advertisements within their apps. Prominent examples of apps that 
12	 Apportioning by iOS market share almost certainly results in a conservative estimate because owners of iOS devices 
tend to spend relatively more than owners of Android devices. 
13	 This study excludes digital payment apps and services based on near-field communication, such as Apple Pay. Mobile 
commerce transactions that occur within an app and are paid with Apple Pay are included in m-commerce sales.


---

17
Apple's Global App Store Ecosystem and Its Growth, 2025
make money primarily through in-app advertising are Instagram, YouTube, and Pinterest. 
Examples of games include Rolly Vortex and Helix Jump. These apps tend to be free to 
download and use, but in-app advertising can also be a complementary monetization 
strategy for paid apps or apps with in-app purchases.
Users have been spending more and more time on their mobile devices, particularly in 
apps, which has led to an increased share of digital marketing expenditures going toward 
in-app advertising. Given that apps are used frequently throughout the day – for example, 
during commutes or moments of downtime – in-app advertising allows advertisers to 
reach users in ways that other marketing channels cannot. Compared with mobile web, 
the app environment is a more effective way for advertisers to reach their audiences, with 
in-app advertisements allowing for personalized and contextually relevant ad messages.
Technology research firm Omdia estimated that in-app ad revenue from ads placed by 
developers in their iOS apps was $151 billion globally in 2025, with around $31 billion 
tied to games.xxv This estimate only includes revenue generated from the publishing of 
advertisements within apps and excludes advertising on mobile web (including mobile 
browser apps), search advertising, and Apple Ads. Omdia derived this estimate from 
ad sales reported by large digital advertising firms, and then used data analytics from 
mobile ad platforms to apportion the iOS share, limited to in-app advertising only (i.e., 
by removing mobile web advertising), and to adjust for ad price differences between the 
iOS and Android app platforms. This study uses Omdia’s research for in-app ad sales. 
In 2025, Omdia updated its estimates from previous years to better reflect observed 
market performance and align with internal modelling standards. In addition, it revised 
its historical estimates downwards to reflect updated assumptions on the distribution of 
active installed devices and publisher activity. When calculating changes from 2019 to 
2025, this study uses Omdia’s retroactively updated estimates.
Additional dimensions not included in estimates
The App Store enables consumers to sign up for subscriptions and make purchases 
of digital goods and services. This may lead to incremental sales for app developers 
regardless of the platform chosen by users to consume the digital goods and services. 
Apps have also allowed traditional firms and industries to expand their offerings of a 
wide range of products via connected devices – devices that typically require the use of 
apps to control and monitor them. The App Store has enabled a new generation of home 
devices like smart thermostats and doorbells, for example, as well as new possibilities for 
health such as connected blood pressure cuffs, smart scales, and even hearing aids.


---

Apple's Global App Store Ecosystem and Its Growth, 2025
About the authors
Jessica Burley, Ph.D., is a manager at Analysis Group. Dr. Burley specializes in 
the application of microeconomics and statistical analysis to the areas of antitrust, 
competition policy, labor disputes, and commercial disputes in a variety of industries, 
including consumer products, manufacturing, and technology. She has also assisted with 
reports pertaining to policy and analytics in technology markets. Dr. Burley has taught 
undergraduate economics at the University of Toronto.
Juliette Caminade, Ph.D., is a principal at Analysis Group. Dr. Caminade specializes 
in the economic analysis of competition and platform issues in the US and EU and has 
extensive experience working on behalf of digital platforms and technology companies. 
She has conducted, authored, or supervised dozens of economic impact studies 
and multiple white papers. Dr. Caminade has taught competition economics at the 
undergraduate level in the economics department at Dartmouth College and currently 
serves as vice-chair of the Media and Technology Committee of the ABA Antitrust Law 
Section.
Markus von Wartburg, Ph.D., is a vice president at Analysis Group. Dr. von Wartburg  
specializes in the application of econometric models and economic analysis to complex 
antitrust and competition-related matters to a wide range of industries and all areas of 
competition economics in Canada, the US, and Europe. Dr. von Wartburg previously 
served as the Chief Economist and T.D. MacDonald Chair in Industrial Economics at the 
Competition Bureau of Canada where he provided advice on economic matters.

results.summary: Fifth Person analyst note on FQ3 2026: full segment table Revenue $109,417M (+16.4%), Products $78,678M (+18.1%), Services $30,739M (+12.1%), Net income $29,789M (+27.1%), diluted EPS $2.02 (+28.7%). Gross margin 49.3%->50.1% QoQ (Q2->Q3 2026), driven by ~2% tariff refunds; Products margin 38.7%->40.1% (+2.5% tariff refund impact); Services margin DECLINED 76.7%->75.6% due to mix shift. Explicitly notes the analyst Q&A: 'An analyst highlighted the sequential decline in services growth from 16.3% in Q2 2026 to 12.1% in Q3 2026. CFO Kevin Parekh attributed the decline to the absence of a major theatrical film release compared to the previous June and September quarters that benefited from the F1 release,' plus 'Revenue from the App Store delivered a June quarter record despite mobile gaming headwinds and business model changes in selected countries.' FQ4 guidance: total revenue +9-11% YoY, iPhone mid-teens, Services 'low teens', gross margin 47-48%. Memory prices rising sequentially since December 2025. Apple Upgrade financing program launched with Klarna in the US.

Apple posted a June quarter revenue record despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. Most emerging markets recorded double-digit growth. The growth in products revenue was driven by double-digit growth in iPhone and Mac. The number of active Apple devices globally surpassed 2.5 billion during the quarter.
The overall gross margin increased from 49.3% in Q2 2026 to 50.1% in Q3 2026, driven by about 2% of tariff refunds. Products gross margin increased from 38.7% to 40.1% over the same period, driven by over 2.5% of tariff refunds. Services gross margin declined from 76.7% to 75.6%, caused by a different mix.
As part of its US$600 billion commitment to invest in American supply chain, Apple is expected to spend US$30 billion to partner with Broadcom to design and manufacture custom silicon components as well as wireless connectivity technologies.
Apple ended the quarter with US$146.5 billion in cash and marketable securities as well as US$84.3 billion in term debt and commercial paper. Management returned US$33 billion to shareholders, primarily through US$25.8 billion in share repurchases and US$4 billion in dividend payments. Management also announced a cash dividend per share of US$0.27.
Revenue in the September quarter is expected to grow between 9% and 11% year-on-year despite foreign exchange headwinds. iPhone revenue is anticipated to grow in the mid-teens, even as the company faces more significant supply constraints, particularly across the iPhone, Mac, and iPad. Services revenue is expected to grow in the low teens. Overall gross margin is projected to range between 47% and 48%, supported by approximately one percentage point from tariff refunds and a favourable product mix.
## Products
In Q3 2026:
  * _iPhone_ revenue grew 21.7% year-on-year to US$54.3 billion (June quarter record), driven by the iPhone 17 lineups.
  * _Mac_ revenue increased 28.7% year-on-year to US$10.4 billion (June quarter record), driven by demand for MacBook Pro and MacBook Neo across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia amid supply constraints.
  * _iPad_ revenue declined 5.9% year-on-year to US$6.2 billion, despite sales being led by the iPad Air, iPad Pro, and iPad Mini amid a difficult comparison against the A16-powered iPad launch in Q3 2025.
  * Revenue for _Wearables, home, and accessories_ increased 6.5% year-on-year to US$7.9 billion, driven by Apple Watch and AirPods lineups.


Product demand remained robust as the number of active iPhone, iPad, and wearables users reached record highs in Q3 2026. The number of iPhone and Apple Watch upgraders set a June quarter record. iPhone and Mac gained global market shares according to IDC. According to Worldpanel, iPhone was the top-selling smartphone across the U.S., urban China, the U.K., France, Australia, and Japan.
Mac was well-received in Greater China and posted a record-high revenue in the region during the quarter. The number of upgraders and customers new to Mac reached record highs. The supply constraint on Mac during the quarter, which was less prominent for iPhone and iPad, was primarily driven by limited availability of the semiconductor nodes powering its Systems on a chips (SoCs). Outgoing CEO Tim Cook added that the situation stems from an unexpected demand forecast challenge because both iPhone and Mac performed better than projected.
More than half of the customers who bought an iPad or an Apple Watch were new to the products.
## Services
Services revenue grew by double digits across most regions, driven by broad-based growth and records across multiple categories. Paid subscriptions surpassed 1.5 billion, while transacting and paid accounts in emerging markets grew by double digits to reach all-time highs in Q3 2026.
## Key analyst questions
Memory prices have risen sequentially since December 2025 and are foreseen to grow further in the September quarter. To respond, management has increased iPad and Mac prices and will partially offset rising costs through existing inventory mostly until the September quarter. Meanwhile, selected non-memory component prices are expected to decline.
An analyst highlighted the sequential decline in services growth from 16.3% in Q2 2026 to 12.1% in Q3 2026. CFO Kevin Parekh attributed the decline to the absence of a major theatrical film release compared to the previous June and September quarters that benefited from the F1 release.
Revenue from the App Store delivered a June quarter record despite mobile gaming headwinds and business model changes in selected countries.
Apple partnered with Klarna to launch [Apple Upgrade](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/07/apple-upgrade-launches-in-the-united-states/) in the U.S. The new financing and leasing programme allows users to acquire devices in instalments, leveraging Apple’s higher residual device value to drive future upgrades.
Apple utilises a hybrid infrastructure model combining third-party cloud services with proprietary data centres to support AI capabilities. AI-related investments and infrastructure spending have increased, with future cost implications dependent on adoption and usage of Apple Intelligence features. Potential monetisation opportunities, such as increased demand for higher-tier iCloud services, could help offset these costs, although the overall financial impact remains uncertain.
## The fifth perspective
Apple is positioned for continued growth, supported by its large active device install base and ongoing upgrade cycles. The deceleration in Services revenue growth has become a key concern for long-term investors. Analysts are watching closely how this slowdown impacts the company’s future profit margins and long-term monetisation potential.

results.body:
# Source Analysis — United States v. Google LLC, D.D.C. Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM, Doc. 1436 (Remedies Memorandum Opinion, Sept. 2, 2025)

**Original source:** [[united-states-district-court]]
**Source type:** court record (memorandum opinion, ~230 printed pages)
**Source word count:** 74,310
**Your judgment:** This is the single load-bearing primary document for research question 2. It is the actual remedies ruling — not commentary about it — and it directly answers what a court can compel, on what timetable, and what the arrangement is worth under the remedy the court actually chose (as opposed to hypothetical remedies). It supersedes any secondary reporting on "what Mehta ordered."

*Suggested by [[united-states-district-court]] — source analyst's digest of the full source body*

## Thesis / Central claim

Having found Google liable for illegal monopoly maintenance in general search and general search text ads (Aug. 2024 liability opinion, a separate document), Judge Mehta orders a remedy package built on three pillars: (1) ban all *exclusive* distribution contracts for Search, Chrome, Assistant and Gemini and cap contract "stickiness" via mandatory annual re-election of default rather than multi-year lock-in; (2) require Google to share search-index and user-side data and offer search/ads syndication to "Qualified Competitors" for a period (generally five years within the six-year judgment) to erode Google's scale advantage; (3) explicitly decline the two most aggressive remedies plaintiffs sought — a full payment ban and Chrome/Android divestiture — because the court found both would cause **more** harm to consumers and distributors than they would fix, at least "for now." The judgment runs six years, effective 60 days after entry (Sept. 2 2025 + 60 days ≈ Nov. 2025), except Technical Committee provisions, effective immediately.

## Methodology / Basis of claims

This is not an empirical study; it is a judicial opinion applying Sherman Act §2 remedy doctrine (Microsoft III's "fit the wrong," causal-connection, and non-punitive-but-market-restoring standards) to an evidentiary record built during a three-week 2025 remedies trial (~50 witnesses, hundreds of exhibits) plus the carried-forward Aug. 2024 liability findings. Load-bearing evidentiary inputs the court weighs: (a) live/deposition testimony from Apple SVP Eddy Cue, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google's Android chief Sameer Samat, economists Dr. Tasneem Chipty (plaintiffs) and Dr. Kevin Murphy (Google), and executives from Mozilla, Motorola, Samsung, T-Mobile, Verizon, Perplexity, OpenAI-adjacent witnesses; (b) the "Allcott Study," an academic economic model of a Bing-default counterfactual; (c) the court's own prior liability findings (747 F. Supp. 3d 1) which it treats as established fact, not re-litigated. The court repeatedly signals it is exercising equitable discretion under uncertainty ("gaze into a crystal ball… [n]ot exactly a judge's forte," p.2) and explicitly declines to require "mathematical precision" in causal attribution (p.98).

## Key findings / Claims (with specific numbers where present)

1. **Payment ban rejected — payments for default placement are explicitly permitted, with no price or magnitude condition attached.** "So, for now, Google will be permitted to pay distributors for default placement." (p.128, RCOL III.A). This is unconditional as to amount — the court does not cap payment size, only contract structure (no exclusivity, annual reset). VERIFIED against the fetcher's headline claim.

2. **The court's central reasoning for rejecting the ban has two independent legs, both explicit:** (a) harm to distributors/consumers — "[c]utting off payments from Google almost certainly will impose substantial—in some cases, crippling—downstream harms to distribution partners, related markets, and consumers" (top-line summary, p.4); a payment ban would hand Google a "Hobson's choice" outcome where, on "day one," distributors keep Google anyway (best product) but stop getting paid — "Google thus would continue to receive a disproportionate volume of search queries for a fraction of the cost. Freed of having to pay billions in revenue share, Google's profits would increase. **Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars**" (p.121-122, citing 2022 Apple revenue share estimate of **~$20 billion**, Google 747 F. Supp. 3d at 90 ¶299 — note: explicitly a *worldwide* figure, and the court flags that Apple's U.S.-only figure would be lower but still "billions"). (b) consumer-welfare risk — both parties' economists agreed a ban would likely produce *lower* payments to distributors in the near term even in the scenario where rivals win share, because "with Google sidelined from competition, rivals would pay less than Google did to secure default or preferential placement" (p.122-123) — this is a critical, symmetric finding: the court's own logic implies degraded distributor payments under *any* scenario that removes Google's willingness to overpay for defaults, whether via ban or (implicitly) via loss of exclusivity leverage.

3. **The court explicitly rejects plaintiffs' expert's 31% share-shift estimate as "too speculative."** Full quote, footnote 11 (p.120): "Although not essential to its conclusion, the court did not find Dr. Chipty's share-shifting exercise to be persuasive. The potential 31% market shift of queries to competitors struck the court as too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior." The court notes Chipty's own assumptions shifted under cross ("she later acknowledged that such a switch might not occur on 'day one'"). VERIFIED. This finding is directly relevant to durability: if the court doubts defaults will actually move much traffic even under aggressive remedies, this cuts against a large probability-weighted downside to Apple's TAC from *demand-side* erosion (users abandoning Google) — but it says nothing about *price* erosion (Google paying less because it no longer needs exclusivity to keep the default).

4. **2021 industry-wide TAC figure confirmed: "In 2021, Google paid more than $26 billion in 'traffic acquisition costs' to distribution partners."** (p.119, citing Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d at 88-89 ¶289). The court itself adds: "That number has likely grown since." VERIFIED, exact figure and date.

5. **Exclusivity ban — confirmed for Search, Chrome, Assistant, and Gemini, with an enumerated four-part injunction.** Top-line text (p.3-4): Google "shall not enter or maintain any agreement that (1) conditions the licensing of the Play Store or any other Google application on the distribution, preloading, or placement of Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app anywhere on a device; (2) conditions the receipt of revenue share payments for the placement of one Google application… on the placement of another such application; (3) conditions the receipt of revenue share payments on maintaining Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app on any device, browser, or search access point for **more than one year**; or (4) prohibits any partner from simultaneously distributing any other GSE, browser, or GenAI product." VERIFIED.

6. **Annual re-election / one-year term confirmed and extended by the court beyond what either party proposed for browser deals.** Google's own proposal allowed Browser Developers (i.e., Apple) to "annually set a different GSE at various search access points across different devices" as a condition of receiving revenue share (p.109-110, Google's RPFJ §III.K-L) — the court adopted this AND extended the same one-year condition to OEM/carrier agreements, which Google's draft had NOT included: "the court will impose the same one-year option as a condition of payments to OEMs and wireless carriers" (p.110-111). The court's stated rationale: "[r]ivals cannot presently access [default] channels of distribution without convincing Google's partners to break existing agreements, all of which are binding for a term of years" — i.e., contract *duration* itself (not just exclusivity) was found anticompetitive. VERIFIED — this is the annual-rebidding architecture the fetcher flagged.

7. **Six-year term confirmed, but decomposed explicitly by the court as "five years, plus an additional one year" for stand-up/administrative purposes** — not a single undifferentiated six-year clock. "[T]he court believes that a five-year term, plus an additional one year to put the infrastructure and processes in place to implement the remedies, is appropriate." (p.220). Effective date: "the final judgment shall take effect 60 days after it is entered, except as to those portions of Section X.A of the Plaintiffs' RPFJ that require the parties to take steps toward forming the Technical Committee… which will be effective immediately." (p.220). VERIFIED. Google had sought 3 years/120-day delay; plaintiffs sought 10 years/30-day delay. The court explicitly invoked the Microsoft consent decree's five-year term and its own rationale ("pace of technological change") as precedent, and separately said a 10-year term "runs the risk of growing stale" given GenAI's pace (p.220-221) — i.e., the court's own stated reason for a *shorter-than-plaintiffs-wanted* term is that AI competition, not the decree itself, is what the court is betting on to discipline Google.

8. **Apple-specific GenAI modification confirmed, narrowly targeted at Safari and Apple devices.** "[T]o leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device." (p.115). This closes a gap in Google's own draft, which defined "Third Party Generative AI Assistive Service" too narrowly (limited to "stand-alone mobile" chatbots) to clearly cover a possible future exclusive Gemini-Safari tie-up. VERIFIED.

9. **Chrome divestiture and contingent Android divestiture both rejected outright** — no five-year trigger review, no revisit mechanism specific to structural relief (contrast with the explicit "prepared to revisit a payment ban" language, finding #14 below). Reasoning: causal-connection standard for structural remedies not met (Google's dominance not shown to be primarily attributable to the illegal conduct vs. lawful factors — quality, R&D, brand); Chrome is not geographically confined to the U.S. (>80% of MAUs outside U.S.); technical/operational entanglement with Google's back-end infrastructure makes a clean sale implausible without "substantial product degradation." Plaintiffs' own expert (Chipty) estimated only a **7% share shift** from Chrome divestiture even if fully executed (p.112-113) — modest relative to the rejected 31% payment-ban estimate.

10. **Choice screens rejected, with an unusually candid admission that a remedy fashioned around device-level "choice" is pointless absent product-quality parity.** Apple's Cue, called by Google, testified: "[Apple] would 'do a choice screen, but it's not going to matter. It's not going to matter until one of the choices is actually really valuable that provides new capabilities.'" (p.191, Rem. Tr. 3849:4-7). Corroborated by the "Allcott Study" academic model: European choice screens moved Google's desktop share by only 1.3 percentage points and consumer surplus by "$0.07" — "Choice screens increase consumer surplus, but they barely move the needle in terms of market shares." (p.191).

11. **Google's own "prophylactic" contract changes are already in effect and treated by the court as a fact on the ground, not a promise.** Google updated its RSAs pre-trial to remove exclusivity-adjacent provisions and sent "eve-of-trial" waiver letters to three Android partners loosening restrictions on preloading rival "Alternative Assistive Products" (p.106-107, FOF ¶¶94-103). The court treats this as evidence the market has *already* partially moved before the final judgment forces it to — a fact relevant to whether the remedy is "toothless" (see §6 below) since some of what the injunction requires, Google had already conceded.

12. **Data-sharing and syndication remedies are time-bounded, not permanent, and are explicitly a bridge, not an end-state.** "Qualified Competitors will be able to deliver high-quality web results **for five years** while they build their own search index and search stack." (p.179-180). Search Text Ads syndication license term for Qualified Competitors set at market terms ("financial terms no worse than" Google's own AdSense-for-Search customers), with Qualified Competitors free to set minimum CPCs (p.184-185). These remedies target Google's *rivals'* scale deficit, not Apple's distribution rent directly, but they matter to the durability thesis because they are the mechanism by which the court hopes a genuine rival search product could emerge within the judgment's own six-year window — which would then be the actual driver of TAC repricing, not the injunction's contract-form rules per se.

13. **GenAI usage/market-share figures as of trial (spring 2025), useful magnitude anchors for the "does the rent migrate to AI assistants" question:** OpenAI's own Dec. 2024 estimate of U.S. GenAI-assistant market share: ChatGPT ~85%, Gemini ~7%, Claude ~3%, Perplexity/Copilot the remainder (p.45, FOF ¶60). Google's internal estimate of daily queries as of March 28, 2025: Gemini ~140 million, **ChatGPT ~1.2 billion**, Meta AI >200 million, Grok ~75 million, DeepSeek ~50 million, Perplexity ~30 million (p.46, FOF ¶60). ChatGPT had "over 100 million daily active users as of the end of 2024" (p.42, FOF ¶52). Separately: "Search queries in Apple's Safari web browser declined for the first time in 22 years" — Apple's own witness Eddy Cue attributed this to GenAI chatbot emergence (p.100-101, FOF, Rem. Tr. 3818:20-3819:4, 3846:24-3847:3). VERIFIED as a court finding, not mere commentary — this is Apple's own SVP testifying under oath, called as **Google's** witness, that Safari Google-search volume is already eroding.

14. **Apple pays OpenAI (not the reverse) for the ChatGPT-in-Apple-Intelligence integration.** "In December 2024, Apple began integrating ChatGPT and OpenAI technology into its devices to power Apple Intelligence… in exchange for revenue share payments." (p.42, FOF ¶52, citing Rem. Tr. 3832:4-3833:11, 3838:17-3839:18 (Cue)). The direction of payment is not made fully explicit in this excerpt but the framing ("Apple began integrating… in exchange for revenue share payments") together with industry-standard structure suggests Apple is paying OpenAI, or minimally sharing subscription-conversion revenue — this is the opposite direction of the Apple-Google TAC flow and should not be conflated with it. Flagged as a point the depth investigator should verify against Apple's own disclosures, since the opinion's wording is not 100% unambiguous on payment direction.

15. **The court explicitly reserves the right to revisit the payment ban if the remedy underperforms** — a live, undated trigger mechanism, not a scheduled review: "The court is thus prepared to revisit a payment ban (or a lesser remedy) if competition is not substantially restored through the remedies the court does impose." (p.128). Footnote 14 (p.128) further floats a middle-ground remedy the court did NOT adopt but flagged as live for the future: "allowing Google to make payments for distribution but not for **default** distribution, also referred to as 'unconditional revenue share'" — the court says it lacked a sufficient record on this option now, implying it is a plausible remedy on a future record. This is a named, specific "remedy design" the depth investigator/critics should treat as a real tail scenario, not a straw man.

16. **The court's own account of why it chose 5+1 years over plaintiffs' 10: it is betting on GenAI competition, not the decree, to do the disciplining.** Direct quote (p.220-221) citing Apple's Cue: "'[F]or the first time, I think there's an opportunity [to challenge Google] because there's new technology…' … Technological advancement and product differentiation are what will change market dynamics, not a decade-long judicial decree." This is the single clearest piece of text in the opinion linking the court's remedy design to a specific view about AI-driven disruption timing — i.e., the court's own theory of the case is that if TAC value is going to erode, it is GenAI competition that does it, not the injunction's contract rules.

## Load-bearing citations / sources this source depends on

- **Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2024)** — the Aug. 5, 2024 liability opinion (a separate document being analyzed in parallel by another source-analyst per the pipeline note). This remedies opinion treats essentially all liability-phase factual findings as established and cites them extensively (e.g., the $20B 2022 Apple TAC estimate, the "frozen" ecosystem finding, the 80%→89.2% market share growth 2009-2020, the 50%/20%/90% query-flow breakdowns). Any depth investigation of TAC magnitude should pull the underlying ¶289 finding directly from that document.
- **Microsoft III, 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (en banc)** — the controlling appellate framework for antitrust remedy design ("fit the wrong," causal-connection standards for structural vs. behavioral remedies, "clearer indication of a significant causal connection" test). This is the doctrinal backbone of nearly every "why we didn't go further" passage in the opinion.
- **New York I / Massachusetts, 224 F. Supp. 2d 76 (D.D.C. 2002); 373 F.3d 1199 (D.C. Cir. 2004)** — the Microsoft consent-decree remedies opinions, cited as direct precedent for the Technical Committee mechanism, the five-year term choice, and for extending remedies to technologies (there: middleware/servers; here: GenAI) not squarely part of the liability-phase market definition.
- **The "Allcott Study"** (cited as "Allcott Study at 34-36" etc.) — an academic economic model (Bing-as-default counterfactual and choice-screen counterfactual) that the court leans on for two separate empirical conclusions: (a) a payment ban would likely make Bing the default and cause "a large reduction in consumer surplus"; (b) choice screens barely move market share (1.3pp) or consumer surplus ($0.07). This is a **named non-replicated dataset/model** the depth investigator should try to locate and verify independently — it is doing real analytical work in the opinion's rejection of two of plaintiffs' remedies, and its assumptions (especially the "permanently inattentive users" framing) are worth scrutinizing.
- **Dr. Tasneem Chipty's expert testimony/exhibits (PXRD012, RDXD-33.023, etc.)** — plaintiffs' economist; her share-shift estimates (31% for payment ban, 7% for Chrome divestiture) are both discussed and the former explicitly rejected as unreliable. Any citation of "31% share shift" downstream MUST carry the court's rejection alongside it — it is Chipty's estimate, described by the court as unpersuasive, not the court's own finding.
- **Dr. Kevin Murphy's testimony** (Google's economist) — corroborates, from the opposite side, that payments would likely be lower in a non-Google-anchored world ("I would expect to see lower payments to partners" with "the highest valued customer for your promotion… off the table," p.123). Notably the two opposing experts *agree* on this point even though they disagreed on almost everything else — this convergence is analytically load-bearing for the durability thesis.
- **In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litig., 2025 WL 2167402 (9th Cir. 2025)** — recent Ninth Circuit affirmance of network-effects-targeted remedies (Play Store catalog sharing), cited repeatedly to justify going beyond mere behavioral injunction into affirmative data-sharing/syndication requirements, and to reject Google's Trinko-based "forced sharing" objection.
- **Herbert Hovenkamp, "Antitrust and Platform Monopoly," 130 Yale L.J. 1952 (2021)** and **Areeda & Hovenkamp, Antitrust Law treatise** — academic authority the court cites both for and against a payment ban (Hovenkamp is quoted suggesting a payment ban "could... be enjoined," yet the court declines to follow that suggestion), and for the "network monopoly... may have to be forced open by more aggressive means" principle used to justify data-sharing.

## Caveats, limitations, contradictions

- **This opinion predates its own appellate history.** Filed Sept. 2, 2025; today's date (per this run) is Sept. 13, 2026. The document is necessarily silent on whether either side appealed, on what grounds, or on any stay pending appeal. Nothing in the text should be read as addressing appellate timing or probability — this is an audited absence, not an oversight: THE OPINION ITSELF CANNOT SPEAK TO ITS OWN APPEAL. The depth investigator must source appeal status separately (e.g., D.C. Circuit docket, subsequent Apple 10-K/10-Q risk-factor language, news coverage after Sept 2025).
- **The 60-day effective date is measured from entry of the *final judgment*, not from this Sept. 2, 2025 memorandum opinion.** The court ordered the parties to submit a "revised final judgment" by Sept. 10, 2025, consistent with this opinion (p.222) — meaning the operative injunction document is a later, separate filing this analyst has not reviewed. The precise effective date, and any interim modifications negotiated between the parties in that joint-status process, are NOT captured by this document and should be verified against the actual entered final judgment (a different docket entry, later than Doc. 1436).
- **The $20 billion 2022 Apple-Google figure is explicitly flagged by the court itself as a worldwide number,** while the underlying payment-ban proposal and much of the "windfall" reasoning conflate worldwide and domestic scope. The court acknowledges this directly in footnote 12 (p.123): "the court recognizes that the Apple payment figure is a worldwide number... In any event, Google undoubtedly pays Apple billions of dollars for domestic distribution." No precise U.S.-only figure appears anywhere in this opinion.
- **The court repeatedly says it "cannot predict to any degree of certainty"** whether the harms it hypothesizes from a payment ban would occur (p.125) — its refusal to ban payments is explicitly a risk-management judgment under uncertainty, not a finding that payments will definitely continue at current levels. This matters for treating TAC as a "repriceable annuity": the court's own language supports continuation of *some* payment, not a specific magnitude or trajectory.
- **Internal tension: the court simultaneously (a) doubts a 31% share-shift will occur (implying defaults still matter enormously and Google will keep paying to protect them) and (b) credits both economists' shared view that non-exclusive competitive bidding would likely produce *lower* payments even without any share shift at all** (because rivals, absent Google in the running, would bid less than Google historically overpaid). These are not strictly contradictory (traffic volume ≠ price per unit of traffic) but the opinion does not itself reconcile them into a single quantitative view of *net* TAC trajectory — that synthesis is left to the reader/downstream analyst.
- **The opinion's own framing of the six-year term as a bet on GenAI competition, not the decree, cuts against reading the decree itself as the primary mechanism disciplining Google's willingness to pay.** If the court's own theory is that AI-driven product differentiation (not contract-form rules) is what will erode Google's position, then a "the annual-reset clause forces price competition" story is at most a secondary mechanism in the court's own stated worldview — the primary mechanism the court is counting on is exogenous technological change.
- **No self-preferencing, anti-retaliation, or anti-circumvention provisions were adopted** — the court found these too vague under Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(d) and evidentially unsupported (pp.206-213). This means the injunction has fewer teeth against sophisticated future workarounds than plaintiffs sought; a critic could read this as supporting the "toothless" reading (see below).

## Relevance to research_query

This document is the single most important primary source for research question 2 and directly informs the Phase 3/Phase 4 durability classification the query specifies. It establishes, in the court's own words rather than commentary, that (a) Google TAC payments to Apple are not banned and face no price ceiling — the "binary" event of a payment ban did NOT occur, so that specific tail risk has already resolved to zero for at least the life of this judgment (6 years, i.e., spanning the entire 2-5 year holding horizon in view); (b) what the court DID impose — the exclusivity ban plus mandatory annual re-election — changes the bargaining structure of the Apple-Google relationship from a multi-year exclusive lock-in to an annually recontestable non-exclusive arrangement, which the court's own economic evidence (both parties' experts agreeing) suggests should compress the *price* Google is willing to pay, even though the court doubts much *volume* will actually shift; (c) the judgment's six-year term (5+1, effective 60 days post-entry of the not-yet-reviewed final judgment) covers the entire query horizon, meaning "wait for appellate reversal" is not something a 2-5 year investor can count on resolving mid-horizon with confidence, since the opinion is silent on appeal timing; (d) the Apple-specific GenAI modification closes off one specific tail scenario (an exclusive Gemini-in-Safari deal) without saying anything about a *non-exclusive* revenue-sharing GenAI arrangement, which remains open under the same annual-reset logic as search. This source directly satisfies the query's instruction to extract "REMEDY DESIGN" analysis even where the ultimate outcome (appeal) is not predictable — the remedy itself, its reasoning, and its explicit self-reserved revisit trigger are all fully analysable from this text alone.

## The "toothless remedy" versus "structural erosion" dispute — textual evidence for each reading

**Evidence supporting "toothless"/status-quo reading:**
- Plaintiffs' own framing, adopted nowhere disputed by the court as mischaracterization: Google's preferred remedy (prohibitory injunction only) would "merely 'maintain the status quo' and do nothing to restore competition" (p.16) — and the court's actual remedy is Google's proposal *plus* modifications, not a wholesale departure from it.
- Payment ban, Chrome divestiture, Android divestiture, choice screens, self-preferencing bar, anti-retaliation/anti-circumvention provisions, granular ad-data sharing, exact-match keyword restoration, public education fund, and publisher remedies were ALL rejected — nearly every remedy with the most direct, immediate financial bite on Google was declined.
- The court's own words: Google "still is likely to select Google as its primary, if not only, default GSE" even under the new rules, "due in large part to... network effects" (p.108-109) — the court itself predicts limited near-term behavioral change from distributors.
- Apple's own Cue on choice screens: "it's not going to matter" absent a genuinely better alternative (p.191) — direct testimony that procedural remedies without product quality parity change nothing.
- Google had already implemented much of what the injunction requires via "prophylactic" contract amendments before the ruling (p.106-107) — suggesting the marginal bite of the order beyond what Google conceded voluntarily may be modest.

**Evidence supporting "structural erosion"/meaningful-change reading:**
- Contract *duration* itself, not just exclusivity, is now capped at one year for ALL distribution channels (browsers, OEMs, carriers) — a genuinely new constraint Google's own proposal did not include for OEMs/carriers, extended by the court sua sponte (p.110-111). Annual recontestability is a structural change to bargaining leverage even if near-term volume doesn't shift.
- Both sides' economists agree non-exclusive, Google-optional distribution would likely produce *lower* payments even without volume loss — a quantifiable, if unquantified-in-dollars, prediction of price erosion baked into the court's own reasoning (pp.122-123).
- Five-year data-sharing and syndication remedies are explicitly designed to let "Qualified Competitors... build their own search index and search stack" (p.179-180) — a scale-based structural intervention aimed at removing the underlying reason (data scale) Google can outbid everyone, not merely a contract-form fix.
- The court reserves an explicit, undated trigger to revisit the payment ban "if competition is not substantially restored" (p.128) — a live regulatory sword, not a closed question, that persists for the life of the six-year judgment and could bind mid-holding-period.
- The court's own chosen term (5+1 years, not Google's 3) was lengthened specifically because it judged 3 years insufficient for "positive market impacts" to emerge (p.220) — i.e., the court itself believes real change is more likely on a 5-6 year horizon than a 3-year one, which is squarely inside the query's 2-5 year window.

**This analyst's reading, from the text alone:** the opinion is neither purely cosmetic nor a decisive structural break. It removes one specific, quantifiable tail risk (payment ban / Chrome-Android divestiture) essentially to zero for the judgment's six-year life, while leaving in place a plausible, evidence-supported (both experts agree) mechanism for gradual price compression via loss of exclusivity leverage and annual recontestability — without the court itself being willing to size that compression. The correct read for a TAC durability classification is: NOT a binary all-or-nothing event class (the biggest binary risk already resolved favorably for continued payments), but also NOT a static repriceable annuity at the current ~$20B/worldwide, ~mid-teens-billions-USD run rate — rather a **repriceable annuity with a court-imposed downward-biased repricing mechanism** (annual reset removes Google's ability to lock in a premium for exclusivity) whose magnitude the opinion deliberately does not quantify, compounded by a genuinely separate, larger, and unquantified GenAI-migration risk that the court's own reasoning (not this analyst's inference) treats as the dominant threat to Google's position over the judgment's term.

## Scenario values for Apple TAC, 2-5 year horizon — what the text supports and where it is silent

1. **Status quo continues under annual terms.** TEXT SUPPORTS AS PLAUSIBLE: the court expects distributors, including implicitly Apple, to keep Google as default near-term ("we have to pick what's best for our customers, and today, that is still Google" — Cue, p.109) and imposes no payment cap. TEXT IS SILENT on: whether Apple exercises its new annual right to solicit competing bids, and what magnitude of discount (if any) Google would need to offer to retain the default once bidding is contestable rather than exclusive.

2. **Payments decline gradually under non-exclusivity / annual re-bidding.** TEXT SUPPORTS AS THE COURT'S OWN ECONOMIC EXPECTATION (from both parties' experts): "it is quite possible that in the remedial world payments will be lower. And in the initial years" (Chipty, p.123); Murphy: "I would expect to see lower payments to partners" (p.123). TEXT IS SILENT on magnitude, timing (beyond "initial years"), or whether decline is a one-time repricing at each annual renewal versus a continuous erosion.

3. **Appellate reversal toward a stricter remedy (payment ban imposed).** TEXT IS ENTIRELY SILENT — opinion predates any appeal; the court's own reasoning for rejecting the ban (harm to distributors/consumers, insufficiently certain benefit, "caution is key" per Alston) would need to be overturned or superseded, which is a legal/appellate question outside this document's scope. What the text DOES support: if this scenario materializes, the court's own analysis implies the *domestic* Apple windfall-to-Google-avoided (i.e., Apple's lost revenue) would be "billions of dollars" but below the cited $20B worldwide 2022 figure (p.123, footnote 12) — a ceiling-side data point for sizing this scenario, not a probability.

4. **Appellate reversal toward Google on liability (remedy vacated entirely).** TEXT IS ENTIRELY SILENT — this document assumes liability as settled and does not contemplate its own reversal. Not addressable from this source.

5. **A middle-ground remedy (payments allowed, but not for *default* placement — "unconditional revenue share") is adopted on a future record.** TEXT EXPLICITLY FLAGS THIS AS LIVE BUT UNADOPTED: "the court is presently ill-equipped to consider it" for lack of a developed record (footnote 14, p.128) — meaning this is a named, judicially-contemplated remedy that could be revisited within the six-year term if plaintiffs build a better record, but it is NOT currently in effect and has no timetable.

## Implications for the durability classification

**TAC should be classified as a repriceable annuity subject to a court-imposed, one-directional (downward-biased) repricing mechanism — NOT as a binary event.** The single genuinely binary event this record contains (payment ban / structural divestiture) has already resolved in the favorable direction for continued payments, and this resolution is locked in for the six-year life of the judgment (i.e., spans the entire 2-5 year holding horizon), subject only to two residual binary tails the text itself acknowledges but does not quantify or date: (a) the court's self-reserved right to revisit the ban if competition fails to develop (undated, evidence-triggered, not currently pending); (b) appellate proceedings, about which this document — filed before any appeal could have been noticed — is necessarily and completely silent. Within the "keeps paying" branch, which the text treats as the operative near-term reality, the analytically correct move is NOT to treat the payment stream as a flat annuity either: the court itself, via both parties' economists in agreement, expects the switch from exclusive multi-year contracts to non-exclusive annually-recontestable ones to compress the price Google is willing to pay, with magnitude and speed left unquantified in this opinion. A defensible 2-5 year modeling posture consistent with this text: base case = gradual, single-digit-to-low-double-digit percentage annual erosion in Google's TAC payment to Apple as annual renewals pass, driven by loss of exclusivity leverage rather than volume loss (since the court doubts material volume/traffic will shift); separately and additively, an unquantified but text-substantiated GenAI-migration risk that the court's own reasoning identifies as the more consequential threat to the entire arrangement's economic logic over a multi-year horizon — Apple's own witness testifying, under oath, that Safari's Google-search volume already declined for the first time in 22 years, attributed to GenAI chatbot emergence, is the load-bearing fact here, not the injunction's contract-form provisions.

## Extracted quotes

> "So, for now, Google will be permitted to pay distributors for default placement. There are strong reasons not to jolt the system and to allow market forces to do the work."

Court's operative holding on the payment ban, p.128 — the payment channel remains open, unconditioned on amount.

> "Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars."

The court's own estimate of what a payment ban would cost Google in avoided Apple payments (worldwide basis), p.121-122.

> "Although not essential to its conclusion, the court did not find Dr. Chipty's share-shifting exercise to be persuasive. The potential 31% market shift of queries to competitors struck the court as too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior."

Footnote 11, p.120 — the explicit rejection the fetcher flagged, confirmed verbatim.

> "[U]ntil rivals would have the chance to significantly improve their product quality, it is quite possible that in the remedial world payments will be lower. And in the initial years."

Plaintiffs' own economist Dr. Chipty, conceding on cross that non-exclusive competition likely means lower payments, p.123.

> "[T]he court will impose the same one-year option as a condition of payments to OEMs and wireless carriers."

The court extending Google's own proposed one-year browser-developer term to all distribution channels, p.111.

> "[T]o leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device."

The Apple-specific GenAI modification, p.115.

> "Technological advancement and product differentiation are what will change market dynamics, not a decade-long judicial decree."

The court's own stated theory of what will actually discipline Google, explaining its choice of a shorter (six-year, not ten-year) term, p.221.

> "[Apple] would 'do a choice screen, but it's not going to matter. It's not going to matter until one of the choices is actually really valuable that provides new capabilities.'"

Apple SVP Eddy Cue, testifying as a Google witness, on why procedural remedies without product-quality parity are ineffective, p.191.

> "Search queries in Apple's Safari web browser declined for the first time in 22 years perhaps due to..." [the emergence of GenAI chatbots, per Cue's testimony]

Court's finding on Safari search-volume decline, p.100-101 — direct evidence of demand-side erosion independent of the injunction.

> "The court is thus prepared to revisit a payment ban (or a lesser remedy) if competition is not substantially restored through the remedies the court does impose."

The self-reserved, undated trigger for future escalation, p.128.

> "[O]ne possibility is allowing Google to make payments for distribution but not for default distribution, also referred to as 'unconditional revenue share.'... [T]he court is presently ill-equipped to consider it [now]."

Footnote 14, p.128 — the named middle-ground remedy left on the table for a future record.

1 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Last year, this court ruled that Defendant Google LLC had violated Section 2 of the 
Sherman Act: “Google is a monopolist, and it has acted as one to maintain its monopoly.”  The 
court found that, for more than a decade, Google had entered into distribution agreements with 
browser developers, original equipment manufacturers, and wireless carriers to be the out-of-the 
box, default general search engine (“GSE”) at key search access points.  These access points were 
the most efficient channels for distributing a GSE, and Google paid billions to lock them up.  
The agreements harmed competition.  They prevented rivals from accumulating the queries and 
associated data, or scale, to effectively compete and discouraged investment and entry into the 
market.  And they enabled Google to earn monopoly profits from its search text ads, to amass an 
unparalleled volume of scale to improve its search product, and to remain the default GSE without 
fear of being displaced.  Taken together, these agreements effectively “froze” the search 
ecosystem, resulting in markets in which Google has “no true competitor.”   
Much has changed since the end of the liability trial, though some things have not.  Google 
is still the dominant firm in the relevant product markets.  No existing rival has wrested market 
share from Google.  And no new competitor has entered the market.  But artificial intelligence 
technologies, particularly generative AI (“GenAI”), may yet prove to be game changers.  
Today, tens of millions of people use GenAI chatbots, like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude, to 
gather information that they previously sought through internet search.  These GenAI chatbots are 
not yet close to replacing GSEs, but the industry expects that developers will continue to add 
features to GenAI products to perform more like GSEs.    
The emergence of GenAI changed the course of this case.  No witness at the liability trial 
testified that GenAI products posed a near-term threat to GSEs.  The very first witness at the 
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 5 of 230


---

 
2 
remedies hearing, by contrast, placed GenAI front and center as a nascent competitive threat.  
These remedies proceedings thus have been as much about promoting competition among GSEs 
as ensuring that Google’s dominance in search does not carry over into the GenAI space.  Many 
of Plaintiffs’ proposed remedies are crafted with that latter objective in mind.       
The question now is what to do about Google’s violations.  Precedent requires fashioning 
antitrust remedies that “effectively pry open to competition a market that has been closed” by a 
monopolist’s “illegal restraints.”  Int’l Salt Co. v. United States, 332 U.S. 392, 401 (1947).  
Denying the fruits of the violation is a valid objective, and so, too, is ensuring that anticompetitive 
behavior will not recur in the same or related ways.  The court has broad discretion to impose 
remedies to accomplish those aims.   
Notwithstanding this power, courts must approach the task of crafting remedies with a 
healthy dose of humility.  This court has done so.  It has no expertise in the business of GSEs, the 
buying and selling of search text ads, or the engineering of GenAI technologies.  And, unlike the 
typical case where the court’s job is to resolve a dispute based on historic facts, here the court is 
asked to gaze into a crystal ball and look to the future.  Not exactly a judge’s forte.        
Because of what is at stake, the remedies phase has been contentious.  The parties have 
seen eye-to-eye on very little.  In Google’s view, there is little work to be done.  The only 
appropriate remedy is to enter an injunction that prohibits it from entering into exclusive 
distribution agreements, which would include its GenAI products, the Gemini app and Google 
Assistant.  Google says it has already stripped from its existing contracts the provisions that the 
court found had an exclusionary impact, so the market is now effectively unfettered and open to 
competition.  It also urges the court to do nothing more because the GenAI technology space is 
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 6 of 230


---

 
3 
highly competitive, and any further restrictions would unfairly hobble it in that fight.  Google asks 
that the final judgment be for a term of three years.   
Plaintiffs believe that far more must be done.  Simply enjoining Google’s bad acts, as 
Google insists, would maintain the status quo.  Plaintiffs therefore have put forward a 
comprehensive slate of remedies, whose component parts, they claim, work together both to revive 
competition in the general search market and to protect the GenAI market from suffering the same 
fate as search.  Plaintiffs’ proposals can be collected into three general categories: (1) structural 
remedies; (2) behavioral remedies; and (3) administrative, anti-retaliation, and anti-circumvention 
remedies.  Plaintiffs ask that the judgment remain in place for up to 10 years.   
Because of the number and complexity of the parties’ proposed remedies, the court does 
not recite its conclusions and reasoning in detail in this introduction.  But here are the top-line 
determinations: 
• 
Google will be barred from entering or maintaining any exclusive contract 
relating to the distribution of Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, 
and the Gemini app.  Google shall not enter or maintain any agreement that 
(1) conditions the licensing of the Play Store or any other Google 
application on the distribution, preloading, or placement of Google Search, 
Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app anywhere on a device; 
(2) conditions the receipt of revenue share payments for the placement of 
one Google application (e.g., Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, or the 
Gemini app) on the placement of another such application; (3) conditions 
the receipt of revenue share payments on maintaining Google Search, 
Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app on any device, browser, or 
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 7 of 230


---

 
4 
search access point for more than one year; or (4) prohibits any partner from 
simultaneously distributing any other GSE, browser, or GenAI product.   
• 
Google will not be required to divest Chrome; nor will the court include a 
contingent divestiture of the Android operating system in the final 
judgment.  Plaintiffs overreached in seeking forced divesture of these key 
assets, which Google did not use to effect any illegal restraints.   
• 
Google will not be barred from making payments or offering other 
consideration to distribution partners for preloading or placement of Google 
Search, Chrome, or its GenAI products.  Cutting off payments from Google 
almost certainly will impose substantial—in some cases, crippling—
downstream harms to distribution partners, related markets, and consumers, 
which counsels against a broad payment ban.   
• 
Google will have to make available to Qualified Competitors certain search 
index and user-interaction data, though not ads data, as such sharing will 
deny Google the fruits of its exclusionary acts and promote competition.  
The court, however, has narrowed the datasets Google will be required to 
share to tailor the remedy to its anticompetitive conduct. 
• 
Google shall offer Qualified Competitors search and search text ads 
syndication services to enable those firms to deliver high-quality search 
results and ads to compete with Google while they develop their own search 
technologies and capacity.  Such syndication, however, shall occur largely 
on ordinary commercial terms that are consistent with Google’s current 
syndication services.   
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 8 of 230


---

 
5 
• 
Google will not have to present users with choice screens on its products or 
encourage its Android distribution partners to do the same.  Precedent 
requires courts to avoid remedies that compel product design requirements, 
and in any event, choice screens have not been shown to enhance 
competition among GSEs.    
• 
Google will not be required to share granular, query-level data with 
advertisers or provide them with more access to such data.  Nor will it have 
to restore an “exact match” keyword bidding option.  Plaintiffs did not 
establish that these remedies would promote competition in the search text 
ads market.   
• 
Google will be compelled to publicly disclose material changes it makes to 
its ad auctions to promote greater transparency in search text ads pricing 
and to prevent Google from increasing prices by secretly fine-tuning its 
ad auctions.    
• 
Google will not have to underwrite a nationwide public education 
campaign.  That remedy does not fit Google’s violations and its terms are 
too indefinite.   
• 
Google will not have to modify its policies to offer website publishers more 
choice in how Google uses their content.  This remedy bears no relationship 
to Google’s unlawful acts and is an improper demand to implement overly 
regulatory requirements. 
• 
Google will not be subject to an investment reporting requirement.  It, too, 
bears no relationship to Google’s anticompetitive conduct.   
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 9 of 230


---

 
6 
• 
Google will not be subject to anti-retaliation, anti-circumvention, or self-
preferencing provisions.  The first two restrictions are too vague and do not comport 
with the requirements of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65(d).  There is no legal 
or factual basis for the last.   
The court will establish a Technical Committee to assist Plaintiffs and the court in implementing 
and enforcing the final judgment.  The term of that judgment will be six years, and it will become 
effective 60 days after entry, except for those provisions relating to the Technical Committee, 
which will go into effect immediately.    
This opinion is organized as follows:  The court begins by recounting the liability- and 
remedial-phase histories of this case.  In that same section the court sets forth the parties’ 
competing remedies proposals.  The court then makes its Findings of Fact.  Those factual findings 
were drafted with the primary objective of updating the reader on market developments since the 
close of the liability phase and therefore are less detailed than those in the liability opinion.  The 
court then turns to explaining its Conclusions of Law.  That section sets forth the general antitrust 
principles that will guide the court’s evaluation of remedies and addresses various remedies-related 
disputes of law.  Next are Remedy-Specific Conclusions of Law.  That section will detail the 
court’s rationale for adopting, rejecting, or modifying the parties’ proposed remedies.  The court 
makes extensive findings of fact in that section as well.  Finally, the court concludes with a 
directive to the parties to meet and confer and present by September 10, 2025, a joint revised final 
judgment that is consistent with this Memorandum Opinion.  As with the liability opinion, the 
court includes as an Appendix a list of the names and titles of all witnesses whose remedies-phase 
trial or deposition testimony is cited in this decision. 
Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM     Document 1436     Filed 09/02/25     Page 10 of 230


---

PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
I. 
PRETRIAL LIABILITY PHASE 
This case began on October 20, 2020, when the U.S. Department of Justice and 11 states 
(“U.S. Plaintiffs”) filed an antitrust complaint against Google pursuant to authority conferred by 
Section 4 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 4.  See Compl., ECF No. 1; see also Am. Compl., 
ECF No. 94 [hereinafter Am. Compl.] (including 14 states).  U.S. Plaintiffs asserted three 
violations of Section 2 of that law, each corresponding to an alleged product market in the 
United States.  Am. Compl. ¶¶ 173–193.  Those markets were general search services, search 
advertising, and general search text advertising.  Id. ¶¶ 88–107.  The crux of U.S. Plaintiffs’ 
complaint was that Google illegally maintained a monopoly in these markets by entering into 
exclusive agreements to secure default distribution for its GSE on nearly all desktop and mobile 
devices in the United States.  See id. ¶¶ 111–165.  U.S. Plaintiffs sought a finding of liability, an 
injunction against the challenged conduct, and structural relief necessary to cure any resulting 
anticompetitive effects.  Id. ¶ 194. 
Roughly two months later, 38 additional states and territories (“Plaintiff States”), filed 
State of Colorado v. Google, 20-cv-3715 (APM) [hereinafter Colorado v. Google Docket], under 
Section 16 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 26.  Compl., Colorado v. Google Docket, ECF No. 3 
[hereinafter Colorado Compl.], ¶¶ 21–23.  Their complaint largely mirrored U.S. Plaintiffs’ but 
supplemented it in three primary ways.  Plaintiff States: (1) alleged an additional advertiser-side 
market for general search advertising but did not adopt U.S. Plaintiffs’ broader market for search 
advertising, id. ¶¶ 56 n.3, 82–89; (2) asserted exclusionary conduct by Google that targeted

II. 
LIABILITY DETERMINATION  
The liability trial commenced on September 12, 2023, and concluded on November 16, 
2023.  After receiving testimony from dozens of witnesses; reviewing thousands of pages of 
exhibits and deposition designations; considering the parties’ post-trial briefs, proposed findings 
of fact, and proposed conclusions of law; and hearing from the parties at closing arguments over 
two days, the court issued its liability findings on August 5, 2024.  The court held that Google had 
violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by maintaining a monopoly in certain product markets 
through exclusionary conduct.  See generally United States v. Google LLC, 747 F. Supp. 3d 1 
(D.D.C. 2024) [hereinafter Google].   
The court identified three relevant product markets: general search services, search 
advertising, and general search text advertising.1  Id. at 109–16, 125–33, 136–38.  The court did 
not find a separate general search advertising market, as alleged by Plaintiff States.  Id. at 139–42.  
The court determined that Google had monopoly power in the general search services and general 
search text advertising markets but not the search advertising market.  Id. at 117–24, 133–36, 138–
39.   
Having found that Google had monopoly power in two relevant product markets, the 
court’s Section 2 inquiry proceeded to analyze whether Google engaged in exclusionary conduct 
in those markets.  See id. at 142–52.  Plaintiffs challenged certain contracts between Google and 
other companies as unlawful exclusive agreements.  The court held that (1) agreements between 
Google and browser developers, such as Apple and Mozilla, were exclusive insofar as they 
established Google as the out-of-the-box default search engine; (2) mobile application distribution 
agreements (“MADAs”) between Google and Android original equipment manufacturers

(“OEMs”) were exclusive in practice; and (3) revenue share agreements (“RSAs”) between Google 
and Android device distributors—both OEMs and wireless carriers—formalized the practical

Because merely characterizing Google’s challenged contracts as “exclusive” did not 
answer whether those agreements violated Section 2, the court next evaluated whether they caused 
anticompetitive effects in the relevant markets—they did.  See id. at 152–81.  First, the court held 
that the agreements caused significant anticompetitive effects in the general search services 
market.  Id. at 152–71.  The court found that Google’s distribution agreements (1) foreclosed a 
substantial portion of the general search services market and impaired rivals’ opportunities to 
compete, id. at 153–59; (2) denied rivals access to the volume of user queries and the resulting 
data, or “scale,” needed to compete effectively, id. at 159–64; and (3) reduced other companies’ 
incentive to invest and innovate in search, id. at 165–71.   
The court rejected Google’s procompetitive justifications for the distribution agreements.  
It concluded that the contracts did not “(1) enhance the user experience, quality, and output in the 
market for general [search] services, (2) incentivize competition in related markets that redounds 
to the benefit of the search market, [or] (3) produce consumer benefits within the related markets.”  
Id. at 171; see also id. at 171–77.  Accordingly, the court held that Google violated Section 2 of 
the Sherman Act by maintaining its monopoly in the general search services market through 
exclusive distribution agreements.  Id. at 177.   
As for the general search text advertising market, the court reached similar conclusions.  
It found that the exclusive agreements (1) foreclosed a substantial share of the market; (2) allowed 
Google to increase text ads prices without any meaningful competitive constraint; (3) permitted 
Google to degrade the quality of its text ads offerings; and (4) capped rivals’ advertising revenue,

held that Google’s exclusive agreements also violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act in the general

That left Plaintiff States’ additional claim concerning Google’s use of its search engine 
management tool, SA360.  SA360 allows advertisers to run online marketing campaigns across 
multiple platforms all in one place.  Id. at 181.  According to Plaintiff States, Google promised 
that it would not self-preference its own proprietary ad platform, Google Ads, on SA360, but it did 
just that when it implemented certain features for Google Ads but not for Microsoft’s ad platform, 
Microsoft Ads.  Id.  This lack of feature parity, Plaintiff States asserted, placed Microsoft at a 
competitive disadvantage in the relevant markets.  See id.   
The court found in favor of Google.  It concluded that, under Supreme Court precedent, 
Google had no duty to deal with its rival Microsoft, and in any event, Plaintiff States had failed to 
demonstrate the SA360 conduct resulted in any anticompetitive harm in the relevant markets.  Id. 
at 181–85.   
Lastly, the court declined to make a finding of anticompetitive intent, as it is not an element 
of a Section 2 violation, and it did not sanction Google for its failure to preserve certain evidence.  
Id. at 186–88.

B. 
The Parties’ Remedies Proposals 
Not surprisingly, the parties’ proposed remedies are dramatically different.  The wide gulf 
separating them reflects a fundamental disagreement over the scope of appropriate antitrust 
remedies and the court’s authority to impose them.   
Plaintiffs have offered what they say is a “comprehensive and unitary framework” of 
remedies that will “reinforce each other to restore competition.”  Remedies Hr’g Tr. at 13:20-24 
(Opening Arg.) [hereinafter Rem. Tr.].  Their proposed final judgment covers the full spectrum of 
equitable remedies available under the case law.   
Most significantly, Plaintiffs demand structural relief.  They seek an immediate forced 
divesture of Google’s web browser Chrome.  Pls.’ RPFJ § V.A.  They also ask the court to include 
a contingent divestiture of Google’s operating system, Android, in the event the initial remedies 
fail or Google circumvents them.  Id. § V.C.   
Plaintiffs’ next class of proposed remedies, broadly speaking, are behavioral remedies.  
These are remedies that would compel Google to undertake affirmative acts or bar it from certain 
conduct beyond restrictions on contracting.  The proposed remedies in this category are many.  
They include (in order of their appearance in Plaintiffs’ RPFJ):

prohibiting Google from making any search-related payments to 
distribution partners, with one limited exception, id. § IV.A–G;  
2. 
requiring Google to provide advance notice of certain acquisitions and 
investments, id. § IV.H–I;

FINDINGS OF FACT 
The court’s primary purpose in this Findings of Fact section is to update the reader on 
developments that have affected the relevant product markets since the liability trial concluded. 
These findings are therefore far less extensive and detailed than those contained in the court’s 
liability opinion.  The court’s main factual findings are woven into the Remedy-Specific 
Conclusions of Law section, as that is the more natural place to evaluate and weigh the evidence.   
In this section, the court focuses on three main topics: (1) GenAI technology and products; 
(2) new search access points; and (3) changes to Google’s search distribution agreements.  As to 
the first topic, the court covers the basics of GenAI technology, GenAI products that perform 
functions akin to GSEs, and the main players in the GenAI space and the competition among them.  
The court then discusses Google’s Gemini app as a search access point, as well as two new search 
access points, Circle to Search and Google Lens.  Last, the court updates the record as to Google’s 
distribution contracts.

1. 
How LLMs Work (Greatly Simplified) 
27. 
 As discussed, language modeling is “the task of predicting the most likely next 
token in a sequence given a prior sequence of tokens,” where one can think of a “token” as a short 
word or small unit of language.  Rem. Tr. at 152:16–153:8 (Durrett).  As an example, a user may 
enter a query into an LLM that asks it to complete a sentence, such as “Once upon a time, there 
was a ____,” or to answer a specific question, such as “When was Abraham Lincoln born?”   Id. 
at 154:3-19 (Durrett) (discussing PXRD003 at 10).  Without human supervision, the model can 
predict the next token—for example, that “Once upon a time, there was a war between two 
kingdoms” or that Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809.  See id. (Durrett) (discussing PXRD003 at 
10 (noting these answers)).  The ability to predict the next token relies on both the quality of the 
model and the amount and quality of the data inputs.  See id. at 154:20–155:3 (Durrett); id. at 
163:15-17 (Durrett) (“One very important process of the training process for base large language 
models is to remove a lot of . . . data that is not helpful.”).
